submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole fires on tokens inside a phrase that specifies a quantity: a number bound to a unit or measure word ('100 degrees', '40 liters', 'two cups', '3 meters', 'eight characters', '500 mg', '3.9 percent'), the amount nouns themselves ('amount', 'quantity'), and the markers that pin an amount to an exact value or a required level ('exactly', 'at least', 'sufficient', 'necessary', 'needed'). Vague degree wording ('quite wide', 'a high temperature', 'about 40 liters') or the same frames carrying no quantity ('add the sugar to the batter') activate it far less.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: On the morning we left, the sky over the harbour was a flat, unbroken grey, and the water lay so still that the moored boats seemed to be resting on glass. My uncle had spent the previous week checking the old trawler from bow to stern, replacing worn lines, tightening the fittings on the cabin roof, and scrubbing the deck until the wood came up pale and clean. He had owned the boat for as long as I could remember, and although he complained about the cost of keeping her afloat, he never once talked about selling. The engine, he said, was the heart of the matter, and an engine that had been neglected was a danger to everyone aboard. We loaded the supplies in the early hours while the gulls argued on the pier: bread, tinned fish, a dented kettle, coils of rope, and a toolbox that rattled whenever the boat rolled. The harbourmaster waved us through the lock and wished us luck. By the time the sun broke through the cloud we were out past the last of the marker buoys, heading north along a coast I had never seen from the water. The cliffs rose in long, layered shelves of grey rock, and now and then a gap in the wall of stone opened onto a beach where nobody had built anything at all. Navigation was my uncle's business. He kept the charts rolled in a tube above the wheel and checked them against the landmarks as we went, muttering to himself whenever the coastline refused to match the paper. The radio crackled with other voices, most of them too faint to follow, and he answered only when a call was clearly meant for us. I sat on the cabin roof for a long while, watching the water change colour as the bottom fell away beneath us, and thinking about how little of the coast I actually knew. By afternoon the wind had picked up and the sea had begun to build. Nothing dramatic, my uncle insisted, but enough that I had to hold on whenever I stood. He reduced speed and turned us further offshore, where the swell was longer and less confused, and we made our way north at a steady pace while the clouds closed over again. It was somewhere off the headland that the engine note changed. My uncle listened for a moment, then went below and came back with a torch, and I followed him down into the cramped, hot space where the machinery lived. He checked the fuel lines, the filters, and the connections on the cooling system, and finally the pressure gauge mounted on the bulkhead beside the pump. It read exactly 3.8 bar, which he said was close enough to normal that we could stop worrying. He topped up the coolant, wiped his hands on a rag, and we went back up into the daylight. The rest of the passage was uneventful. The wind eased after dark, the sea flattened, and the lights of the northern harbour appeared low on the horizon, small and yellow and steady.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout of roughly 600 tokens whose only quantity phrase, 'exactly 3.8 bar', sits deep in the passage, testing whether the quantity feature fires far from the opening of a long document.
